source_text: Τάχα ἀσαφὲς τὸ εἰρημένον· οὐκοῦν αὐτὸ σαφὲς ποιῆσαι πειράσομαι. Ἥμαρτέ τις· ἕτερον ἁμαρτάνοντα τὴν αὐτὴν ἁμαρτίαν κατεδίκασε σφοδρῶς. Ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ οὐ τοσαύτην ἐπισπᾶται κόλασιν, ὅσην ἡ φύσις τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἀπαιτεῖ, ἀλλὰ καὶ διπλασίονα πολλῷ καὶ τριπλασίονα· οὐ γὰρ ἀφ' ὧν αὐτὸς ἥμαρτεν, ἀλλ' ἀφ' ὧν ἕτερον ἁμαρτάνοντα τὰ αὐτὰ χαλεπῶς ἐκόλασε, ψηφιεῖται αὐτῷ τὴν τιμωρίαν ὁ Θεός. Καὶ ὅτι τοῦτό ἐστιν ἀληθὲς, ἀπὸ τῶν γεγενημένων καὶ ἐκβάντων, μειζόνως, ὅπερ ὑπεσχόμην ὑμῖν, αὐτὸ ποιήσω καταφανές. Ὁ Φαρισαῖος, καίτοι γε αὐτὸς οὐδὲν ἁμαρτὼν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν δικαιοσύνῃ ζήσας, καὶ πολλὰ ἔχων κατορθώματα εἰπεῖν, ἐπειδὴ τὸν τελώνην, τὸν ἅρπαγα καὶ πλεονέκτην καὶ παρανομώτατον κατεδίκασε, τοσαύτην ἔδωκε δίκην, ὡς ἐκείνου μείζονι τηρεῖσθαι κολάσει. Εἰ δὲ ὁ μηδὲν μὲν ἁμαρτὼν αὐτὸς, ἁμαρτάνοντα δὲ ἕτερον καὶ περιφανῆ πᾶσιν ἐπὶ παρανομίαις ὄντα, ῥήματι ψιλῷ καταδικάσας τοσαύτην ἐπεσπάσατο κόλασιν, οἱ πολλὰ μὲν καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν ἁμαρτάνοντες, ἑτέρων δὲ βίους καταδικάζοντες, οὐδὲ ἐμφανεῖς ὄντας τινὶ, οὐδὲ δήλους, ἐννόησον ὅσην ὑποστησόμεθα κόλασιν, πῶς ἐκπεσούμεθα πάσης συγγνώμης. Ἐν ᾧ γὰρ κρίματι, φησὶ, κρίνετε, καὶ ὑμεῖς κριθήσεσθε. ςʹ. Διὰ δὴ ταῦτα ἀντιβολῶ, καὶ παραινῶ, καὶ δέομαι, ταύτης ἀποστῆναι τῆς πονηρᾶς συνηθείας. Τοὺς μὲν γὰρ ἱερέας κακῶς ἀκούοντας οὐδὲν παραβλάψομεν, οὐ μόνον ἂν ψευδῆ τὰ λεγόμενα ᾖ, ἀλλὰ κἂν ἀληθῆ· ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ Φαρισαῖος τὸν τελώνην οὐδὲν κατέβλαψεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὠφέλησε, καίτοι γε ἀληθῆ περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἑαυτοὺς τοῖς ἐσχάτοις περιβαλοῦμεν κακοῖς· ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ Φαρισαῖος καθ' ἑαυτοῦ τὸ ξίφος ὤθησε, καὶ καιρίαν πληγὴν λαβὼν ἀπῆλθεν. Ἵνα οὖν μὴ καὶ ἡμεῖς τὰ αὐτὰ πάθωμεν, κρατῶμεν ἀκολάστου γλώττης. Εἰ γὰρ τὸν τελώνην εἰπὼν κακῶς, οὐ διέφυγεν ἐκεῖνος, οἱ τοὺς πατέρας ἡμῶν κακῶς λέγοντες, ποίαν ἕξομεν ἀπολογίαν; εἰ τὸν ἀδελφὸν βλασφημήσασα Μαρία ἅπαξ, τοσαύτην ἔδωκε δίκην, ποίας σωτηρίας ἡμῖν ἐλπὶς, ὅταν μυρίαις καθ' ἑκάστην ἡμέραν τοὺς ἄρχοντας πλύνωμεν λοιδορίαις; Μὴ γάρ μοι τοῦτο λεγέτω τις, ὅτι ἐκεῖνος Μωϋσῆς ἦν· δυνήσομαι γὰρ εἰπεῖν καὶ ἐγὼ, ὅτι κἀκείνη Μαρία ἦν. Ἄλλως δὲ, ἵνα καὶ τοῦτο αὐτὸ μάθῃς σαφῶς, ὅτι εἰ καὶ ἐγκλημάτων ὑπεύθυνοι ὦσιν οἱ ἱερεῖς, οὐδὲ οὕτω σοι θέμις τὸν ἐκείνων βίον κρίνειν, ἄκουσον τί φησι περὶ τῶν ἀρχόντων τῶν Ἰουδαϊκῶν ὁ Χριστός· Ἐπὶ τῆς Μωϋσέως καθέδρας ἐκάθισαν οἱ γραμματεῖς καὶ οἱ Φαρισαῖοι· πάντα οὖν, ὅσα ἂν λέγωσιν ὑμῖν ποιεῖν, ποιεῖτε· κατὰ δὲ τὰ ἔργα αὐτῶν μὴ ποιεῖτε. Καὶ τί γένοιτ' ἂν χεῖρον ἐκείνων, ὧν ὁ ζῆλος ἔφθειρε τοὺς μαθητευομένους; Ἀλλ' ὅμως οὐδὲ οὕτω κατεβίβασεν αὐτοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς ἀξίας, οὐδὲ εὐκαταφρονήτους ἐποίησεν εἶναι τοῖς ἀρχομένοις· καὶ μάλα εἰκότως. Εἰ γὰρ ταύτης ἐπιλάβοιντο τῆς ἐξουσίας οἱ ἀρχόμενοι, ὀφθήσονται πάντας ἀποχειροτονοῦντες, καὶ ἐκ τοῦ βήματος καταβιβάζοντες. Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ Παῦλος τὸν ἀρχιερέα τῶν Ἰουδαίων ὑβρίσας, καὶ εἰπὼν, Τύπτειν σε μέλλει ὁ Θεὸς, τοῖχε κεκονιαμένε· καὶ σὺ κάθῃ κρίνων με; ἐπειδή τινων ἤκουσεν ἐπιστομιζόντων αὐτὸν, καὶ λεγόντων, Τὸν ἀρχιερέα τοῦ Θεοῦ λοιδορεῖς; δεῖξαι βουλόμενος, ὅσην ἀπονέμειν δεῖ τοῖς ἄρχουσι τὴν αἰδῶ καὶ τὴν τιμὴν, τί φησιν; Οὐκ ᾔδειν ὅτι ἀρχιερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἦν.
thought_title: The measure of judgment and the honor due to priests
orientation: Chrysostom is explaining why judging others makes one's own sins worse, then turns to the duty of honoring priests even when they are blameworthy.
pass_a_gloss: Perhaps the thing said is unclear; therefore I will try to make it clear. Someone sinned; he condemned another person sinning the same sin severely. On that day he draws upon himself not so great a punishment as the nature of the sin demands, but even double and triple by far; for not from what he himself sinned, but from what he harshly punished another sinning the same things, God will vote for him the penalty. And that this is true, from the things that have happened and turned out, more forcefully, just as I promised you, I will make it manifest. The Pharisee, although he himself had not sinned, but even had lived in righteousness, and had many successes to speak of, since he condemned the tax collector, the robber and greedy man and most lawless one, he paid such a penalty as to be kept in store for a punishment greater than that man's. But if the one who had not sinned himself, but condemned another sinning and being manifest to all in lawless deeds, with a bare word, drew upon himself so great a punishment, those who sin many things each day, and condemn the lives of others, not even being evident to anyone, nor clear, consider how great a punishment we will undergo, how we will fall away from all pardon. For with what judgment, he says, you judge, you also will be judged. 6. For these very reasons I entreat, and exhort, and beg, to stand away from this wicked habit. For the priests who are spoken of badly we will not harm at all, not only if the things said are false, but even if true; since also the Pharisee did not harm the tax collector at all, but even helped him, although saying true things about him; but we will clothe ourselves in the last evils; since also the Pharisee thrust the sword against himself, and having received a fatal wound he departed. So that we also may not suffer the same things, let us restrain the unbridled tongue. For if the one who spoke badly of the tax collector did not escape, we who speak badly of our fathers, what defense will we have? If Mary, having slandered her brother once, paid such a penalty, what hope of salvation is there for us, when with ten thousand revilings each day we wash the rulers? For let no one say this to me, that that man was Moses; for I will be able to say also, that that woman was Mary. But otherwise, so that you may learn this very thing clearly, that even if the priests are liable to charges, not even so is it lawful for you to judge their life, hear what Christ says about the rulers of the Jews: Upon the seat of Moses sat the scribes and the Pharisees; all things therefore, as many as they say to you to do, do; but according to their works do not do. And what could be worse than those men, whose zeal corrupted the disciples? But nevertheless not even so did he bring them down from their dignity, nor did he make them easily despised by the ruled; and very reasonably. For if the ruled should lay hold of this authority, they will be seen deposing everyone, and bringing them down from the judgment seat. Therefore also Paul, having insulted the high priest of the Jews, and having said, God is about to strike you, whitewashed wall; and do you sit judging me? since he heard some silencing him, and saying, Do you revile the high priest of God? wishing to show how much reverence and honor one must assign to rulers, what does he say? I did not know that he was high priest of God.

choices.term: ψηφιεῖται αὐτῷ τὴν τιμωρίαν ὁ Θεός
choices.english: God will vote for him the penalty
choices.why: ψηφίζω is literally 'to vote' or 'to decree by vote'; keeping 'vote' preserves the judicial metaphor of God as judge rendering a verdict, which Chrysostom is developing
rejected: God will assign him the punishment

choices.english: as to be kept in store for a punishment greater than that man's
choices.why: ἐκείνου refers to the tax collector; the Pharisee's stored-up punishment exceeds the tax collector's, which is the point of the comparison
rejected: as to be kept for a greater punishment than his own
as to be reserved for a punishment greater than that one

choices.english: we will clothe ourselves in the last evils
choices.why: περιβάλλω is literally 'to throw around, clothe'; the middle voice with κακοῖς means to wrap oneself in evils, a vivid image Chrysostom uses for self-inflicted harm
rejected: we will surround ourselves with the worst evils
we will incur the utmost evils

choices.english: having received a fatal wound he departed
choices.why: καιρία πληγή is a mortal or well-aimed blow; 'fatal wound' captures the self-destructive result of the Pharisee's judgment
rejected: having received a timely blow he went away
having taken a critical wound he left

choices.english: let us restrain the unbridled tongue
choices.why: κρατέω with genitive means 'to master, control'; ἀκόλαστος is 'unbridled, licentious', a strong moral term Chrysostom applies to the tongue
rejected: let us hold back an undisciplined tongue
let us rule over a loose tongue

choices.english: we wash the rulers with revilings
choices.why: πλύνω is literally 'to wash'; the image of drenching someone with abuse is vivid and should be kept literal
rejected: we flood the rulers with insults
we shower the rulers with abuse

pass_b_english: Perhaps what I have said is unclear; so let me try to make it clear. Someone sinned, and he condemned another person committing the same sin with great severity. On that day he will draw upon himself not as much punishment as the nature of the sin demands, but far more, double and triple. For God will reckon to him the penalty not on the basis of what he himself sinned, but on the basis of what he harshly punished another person for sinning in the same way. And that this is true, I will make fully evident to you, as I promised, from things that have happened and come to pass. The Pharisee, although he himself had not sinned but had lived in righteousness and had many right deeds to speak of, because he condemned the tax collector—the robber, the greedy man, the most lawless—paid such a penalty as to be kept in store for a punishment greater than that man's. And if the man who himself had not sinned, but condemned with a mere word another man who was sinning and was notorious to all for his lawlessness, drew upon himself such a punishment, then we who sin many times every day and condemn the lives of others—lives not even evident or clear to anyone—consider how great a punishment we will undergo, how we will fall away from all pardon. For with the judgment you judge, he says, you will be judged (Matthew 7:2).

For these reasons I beg and urge and entreat you to depart from this wicked habit. For we will not harm the priests who are spoken of badly, not only if what is said is false, but even if it is true. Since the Pharisee did not harm the tax collector, but even helped him, although he was saying true things about him. But we will entangle ourselves in the utmost evils. Since the Pharisee thrust the sword against himself, and having received a fatal wound he departed. So that we may not suffer the same things, let us restrain the unbridled tongue. For if he did not escape punishment for speaking badly of the tax collector, what defense will we have, we who speak badly of our fathers? If Mary, having slandered her brother once, paid such a penalty, what hope of salvation is there for us, when every day we wash the rulers with countless revilings? Let no one say to me, 'But that was Moses.' For I will be able to say, 'And that was Mary.' But in another way, so that you may learn this very thing clearly—that even if the priests are liable to charges, it is still not lawful for you to judge their life—hear what Christ says about the Jewish rulers: The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat; so do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works (Matthew 23:2-3). And what could be worse than those men, whose zeal corrupted those being taught? But nevertheless he did not bring them down from their dignity, nor did he make them easy to despise by those under their rule. And very reasonably so. For if those under rule seized this authority, they would be seen deposing everyone and bringing them down from the judgment seat. Therefore Paul too, when he insulted the high priest of the Jews and said, God is about to strike you, you whitewashed wall; and do you sit judging me? (Acts 23:3), when he heard some rebuking him and saying, Do you revile God's high priest? (Acts 23:4), wishing to show how much respect and honor one must assign to rulers, what does he say? I did not know that he was God's high priest (Acts 23:5).

problems.why: ψηφιεῖται means 'reckons/counts' not 'votes'; archaic but wrong sense.
problems.fix: God will reckon to him the penalty

problems.quote: clothe ourselves in the last evils
problems.fix: we will entangle ourselves in the utmost evils
problems.ruling: ἐσχάτοις κακοῖς = 'worst/extreme evils'; 'last evils' misleads readers about meaning.

last_rejected.source_quote: ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ Φαρισαῖος τὸν τελώνην οὐδὲν κατέβλαψεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὠφέλησε, καίτοι γε ἀληθῆ περὶ αὐτοῦ λέγων· ἡμεῖς δὲ ἑαυτοὺς τοῖς ἐσχάτοις περιβαλοῦμεν κακοῖς· ἐπεὶ καὶ ὁ Φαρισαῖος καθ' ἑαυτοῦ τὸ ξίφος ὤθησε, καὶ καιρίαν πληγὴν λαβὼν ἀπῆλθεν.
last_rejected.why: Source uses 'ἐπεί' (since/because) for both Pharisee clauses, showing causation; English renders both as 'Since' but breaks the logical chain by splitting into separate sentences.
last_rejected.fix: Keep the causal structure clear: 'since the Pharisee did not harm... but we entangle ourselves... since the Pharisee thrust the sword...'
last_rejected.ruling: English 'Since...Since...' preserves causal ἐπεί; sentence break is stylistic, not meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: For with the judgment you judge, he says, you will be judged (Matthew 7:2).
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἐν ᾧ γὰρ κρίματι, φησὶ, κρίνετε, καὶ ὑμεῖς κριθήσεσθε.
last_rejected.why: The Greek φησὶ marks God as speaker, not Christ; Matthew 7:2 is Christ quoting God's principle.
last_rejected.fix: For with the judgment you judge, God says, you will be judged.
last_rejected.ruling: φησὶ is generic 'he says'; no speaker specified. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: we who speak badly of our fathers
last_rejected.source_quote: οἱ τοὺς πατέρας ἡμῶν κακῶς λέγοντες
last_rejected.why: πατέρας here means spiritual fathers/priests, not biological fathers; context is about clergy.
last_rejected.fix: we who speak badly of our fathers [i.e., priests]
last_rejected.ruling: πατέρας can mean fathers broadly; context clarifies clergy. Not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: whose zeal corrupted those being taught

last_rejected.why: ὁ ζῆλος refers to the Pharisees' teaching/zeal, but 'corrupted' is too strong; ἔφθειρε means 'destroyed/ruined.'
last_rejected.fix: whose zeal destroyed those under their teaching
last_rejected.ruling: ἔφθειρε includes 'corrupted/destroyed'; within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: on the basis of what he harshly punished another person for sinning in the same way.
last_rejected.source_quote: ἀφ' ὧν ἕτερον ἁμαρτάνοντα τὰ αὐτὰ χαλεπῶς ἐκόλασε,
last_rejected.why: Ungrammatical calque of ἀφ' ὧν; obscures that God measures the penalty by the severity of the punishment he inflicted on another.
last_rejected.fix: on the basis of the harsh punishment he inflicted on another person for committing the same sin.
last_rejected.ruling: English keeps ἀφ' ὧν contrast and χαλεπῶς as 'harshly'; awkward wording, meaning not lost or inverted.
